sentences.text: The office was not what she expected, and it took her four visits before she was let far enough in to see any of it properly.
The entrance under the root opens after about a metre and a half into a chamber that a person can sit up in if they do not mind their hair in the roof.
It is dry.
That was the first shock: it is completely dry, in a wood, in November, and Orla never worked out how.
The second shock was the light.
There is some.
Not much — enough to see shapes by after your eyes have had four or five minutes — and it does not come from anywhere.
There is no gap in the roof; she looked, on three separate visits, with a torch, thoroughly.
The light is simply the amount of light there is in that chamber, and it is the same at eleven in the morning and at half past four in December.
The things are in the walls.
Not piled.

Set into the earth in rows, each one pressed into its own small socket, the way you would set eggs into a box, and the rows go round the chamber and back into two passages that Orla was never allowed down.
She counted a hundred and seventeen things on her fourth visit before she gave up counting.

Counting was hard because the sockets go back into the passages and because she was not allowed to move anything, which was made clear to her early and unmistakably on the third visit when she reached for a key and got a noise she did not need translated.
A spectacle case.
Four knives.
A shoe.
A child's shoe and separately a man's boot, not a pair, not near each other.
A watch that was not her grandfather's.
A brooch.
A key with a wooden tag.
Six or twelve coins, none of them together.
A comb.
A thing that turned out, when she got a proper look at it, to be a set of false teeth.
And the catalogue.
The catalogue is on the floor of the chamber and it is not written and it is not a book.
It is marks.
There are marks on the packed earth of the floor, hundreds of them, in rows, cut in with a claw and re-cut, and each mark is directly below the socket of the thing it belongs to.
Orla could not read it and never learned to.

What she learned instead — over about six weeks, by pointing at things and being answered in the only way available, which was that the badger would take a thing out of the wall and turn it and put it back — was what the catalogue was *for*.
It was not an inventory.
It did not say what the thing was.
She established that beyond doubt when she pointed at the false teeth and got shown, in the marks, something nine strokes long.
It said what the thing had been doing when it was lost.
That sentence took her three weeks to arrive at and about a year to believe, and she would like to set out the evidence, because it sounds like something a child decided and it was not.
Two identical objects had different entries.
There were two ordinary iron keys in that wall, the same size, the same pattern, almost certainly from the same kind of lock.
One had an entry of four strokes.
The other had an entry of nine.
And one entry served two completely different objects.
The comb and one of the coins had the same mark under them — she checked this four times, on different days, from different angles, and once lay flat on the floor with a torch to be sure.
Whatever the catalogue was recording, it was not what the things were.
